Concluding Thoughts on Institutional Impediments 
to Executive “Unitariness”
A recurring theme of this chapter has been the “unitary executive” 
debate—^that is, whether the president should be understood to have 
constitutionally vested authority to exert policy control over the exercise of 
discretion by any and every other administrator within the executive 
branch. Whatever the merits of the arguments based on legality, 
accountability, and responsiveness, the sheer complexity of the “executive 
estabhshment,” as we have reviewed it, casts obvious doubt on the capacity 
of any president—^whatever his constitutional prerogatives—to make the 
entire executive estabhshment move in a single well-coordinated, coherent 
pohcy direction. To quote Professor Sunstein again, “[W]hile the President 
is ultimately in charge,” even “the White House itself is a ‘they,’ not an ‘it.’ ” 
Sunstein, supra, 126 Ha r v . L. Re v . at 1840. An “executive estabhshment,” 
as the Administrative Conference caUs it, that comprises hundreds of 
agencies and mihions of officers and employees, quite obviously poses 
chahenges for any hope of tight, hierarchical control.
Some of the resistance to presidential control is built into our 
constitutional design. Professor Saikrishna Prakash, who is generally 
supportive of a unitary executive reading of the Constitution, has written: 
“[UJnitary executivists have neglected the Constitution’s various 
constraints on the President’s abihty to control law execution and the 
extent to which Congress can make the task of presidential control difficult, 
if not impossible.” Saikrishna B. Prakash, Fragmented Features of the 
Constitution’s Unitary Executive, 45 WILLAMETTE L. Re v . 701, 701—702 
(2008—2009). He argues that “Congress exercises significant control over 
the executive branch via its powers to create offices and departments and 
to fund the executive branch. Additionally, the Senate influences who 
becomes officers within these departments, limiting the President’s ability 
to select his most favored choices. Finally, Congress creates the laws that 
executive officers enforce, thereby constraining the discretion of executive 
officers.” Id. at 721—22. In response to these aspects of our constitutional 
structure, we have seen how presidents deploy the powers at their disposal 
to strengthen their position. Over time, presidents have made innovative 
use of executive orders to create new coordination mechanisms within the 
executive branch such as the Domestic Policy Council or the National 
Economic Council, by enlarging the staff of the Executive Office of the 
President, by more carefully screening even lower-level political 
appointees, and by seeking and carefully deploying reorganization 
authority to reshape the executive branch. See Jason Marisam, The 
President’s Agency Selection Powers, 65 Ad min . L. Re v . 821 (2013).
